events.description: Droukdel reportedly killed in a French counterterrorism operation.
Florence Parly tweets Droukdel's death and says he was on al-Qaeda's management committee.
Droukdel assumes leadership of the GSPC.
Droukdel pledges bayah to bin Laden, accepted by Zawahiri.
GSPC rebranded as AQIM (late 2006/early 2007).
Zawahiri sends Droukdel a five-page letter commenting on the GSPC/AQIM charter.
Zawahiri letter to Droukdel asking AQIM to agitate against Denmark over the cartoons.
Droukdel tells the New York Times that Zarqawi helped broker the GSPC merger.
US Navy SEAL raid kills bin Laden in Abbottabad and seizes his files.
Younis al-Mauritani captured in Pakistan.
US Treasury designates Younis al-Mauritani.
Qasim al-Rimi killed.

AQIM-Mauritania truce proposed by Droukdel, approved by al-Qaeda leadership, confirmed by Abu Hafs. Terms: one year, 10-20 million euros annually, no attacks or kidnappings, AQIM allowed to proselytize and use Mauritania as a rear base.
ODNI releases bin Laden files in batches between 2015 and 2017.
Letter from Zawahiri to Droukdel (discussed earlier in episode).
Zawahiri letter to Droukdel relaying bin Laden's instructions to agitate against Denmark over the cartoons; also sent to Islamic State of Iraq leaders.
Droukdel reportedly killed, per France and US Africa Command.
Qasim al-Raymi killed in Yemen; replaced by Khalid Batarfi.
Asim Umar killed in Musa Qala, Helmand.
US-Taliban withdrawal agreement signed.
Taliban Pashto statement denying al-Qaeda presence in Afghanistan, after McKenzie's remarks.
AQAP occupied large areas of southern and central Yemen; Wuhayshi later wrote an after-action report to Droukdel.

key_claims: The hosts say AQIM is part of al-Qaeda, citing the bayah, the bin Laden files and leadership overlap.
The French said Droukdel was on al-Qaeda's management committee and was Zawahiri's third deputy; AFRICOM did not confirm this.
Zawahiri has long managed al-Qaeda's regional branches, including AQIM, and bin Laden asked to be copied through him.
Al-Qaeda leaders reviewed and revised AQIM's and the Pakistani Taliban's charters, indicating a high degree of direction.
Al-Qaeda approved an AQIM truce with Mauritania, with annual payments of 10-20 million euros and freedom to proselytize, and it took effect.
Al-Qaeda is more strategically sophisticated than ISIS because it uses diplomacy and truces to pursue its caliphate goal.
Younis al-Mauritani linked AQIM to al-Qaeda's external operations and was captured in Pakistan in 2011, showing al-Qaeda's Pakistan network remained active.
Al-Qaeda's target-selection guidance covers both local and global enemies while seeking to avoid civilian casualties.
The Pakistani Taliban is effectively an unofficial al-Qaeda branch, and al-Qaeda directed its charter and told it to stop poaching al-Qaeda cadres.
The bin Laden files show al-Qaeda's senior leadership closely directing affiliates such as AQIM and the Islamic State of Iraq.
Al-Qaeda leadership oversaw AQIM hostage ransom negotiations and aimed to pressure France over Afghanistan.
Wuhayshi's after-action report to Droukdel shows al-Qaeda's emirate-building focus and branch-to-branch connectivity.
The claim that al-Qaeda is not interested in territory or a caliphate is contradicted by files and by its actions in Yemen, Mali, Somalia, and Waziristan.
The Taliban's denial that al-Qaeda is in Afghanistan is false, as shown by Asim Umar's death in Helmand, and undermines the US-Taliban counterterrorism assurances.
Droukdel's death does not end AQIM's West African caliphate project, as it has a deep bench of experienced leaders.
